explanations.explanation: That's the one. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, “Consecrate to Me every firstborn male.” (Exodus 13:2) It covers the firstborn from every womb among the Israelites, man and beast. Clear instructions, friend. I wish my recipes came that clear.

Close to a counting rule, but that's not this one. Counting off every tenth is a system for a big pile of cookies, not what the LORD asks here. He asks for the firstborn, the one who opens the womb first. Moses, Israel's leader, hears it in Exodus 13:2.

Nope, nobody's being asked to hand over the person running the house. The LORD says “Consecrate to Me every firstborn male.” (Exodus 13:2) It's about who was born first, not who's in charge of the kitchen. And believe me, the one in charge of the kitchen is NOT always the oldest.

Careful, the LORD doesn't leave the animals out. He says, “The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast.” (Exodus 13:2) So it's people AND animals. Easy one to skim past, friend. I've skimmed past a whole line of a recipe and ended up with a cookie that could break a window.

Right, and the text says so outright. The LORD says the firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Him, “both of man and beast.” (Exodus 13:2) Animals are in it, not just people. Nobody gets left off this list.

explanations.answer: The day they came out of Egypt
explanations.explanation: That's it. Moses tells the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; for the LORD brought you out of it by the strength of His hand.” (Exodus 13:3) It's a day worth remembering. The reason is right there in the verse: the LORD's hand brought them out.

explanations.answer: The names of the twelve tribes
explanations.explanation: Good thing to know, but these verses don't ask for it. Moses says, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt…” (Exodus 13:3) The thing to remember is a day, not a roll call. Tribe names would be a lot of nametags anyway.

explanations.answer: The night they spent in Goshen
explanations.explanation: Goshen doesn't come up in these verses at all. Moses points the people to a different day: the day they came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery (Exodus 13:3). He's pointing them forward, not back to a night in Goshen. And I'd say they're glad to be leaving.

explanations.answer: In the land He swore to their fathers
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says that when the LORD brings them into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites and Jebusites, “the land He swore to your fathers that He would give you,” they will keep this service in this month (Exodus 13:5). So it's a promise they're walking toward. They haven't arrived yet.

explanations.answer: Back in the land of Goshen
explanations.explanation: Nobody's going back. Moses says they'll keep this service once the LORD brings them into the land He swore to their fathers (Exodus 13:5). They're leaving Egypt, and this is about where they're headed. Going back isn't in the plan, friend.

explanations.answer: Out in the land of Midian
explanations.explanation: Midian never comes up in these verses. Moses says they'll keep this service in the land the LORD swore to their fathers, the land flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 13:5). That's the destination. Midian isn't on this map.
Seven days. Moses says, “For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread…” (Exodus 13:6) A whole week of it. That's a commitment, friend, and I respect a long bake.

A feast. On the seventh day, Moses says, “there shall be a feast to the LORD.” (Exodus 13:6) So the week ends in a celebration. That's the kind of ending I like: you work all week, then you get a party.
Three would be a short week. Moses says seven days of unleavened bread (Exodus 13:6). Three days of it and I'd be asking for a refund on my calendar.

One letter off, and it changes everything! The text says there shall be a feast to the LORD on the seventh day, not a fast (Exodus 13:6). One little letter, and suddenly my cookie jar is out of the picture.
Ten is three days too many. Moses says seven days of unleavened bread, and then the feast to the LORD on the seventh day (Exodus 13:6). The count ends right there, at seven.

It goes wider than the houses. Moses says, “Nothing leavened may be found among you, nor shall leaven be found anywhere within your borders.” (Exodus 13:7) That's the whole territory, not just the kitchen. If I had to clear leaven out of my whole planet, I'd need a bigger broom.

Right, it's bigger than the houses. Moses says, “Nothing leavened may be found among you, nor shall leaven be found anywhere within your borders.” (Exodus 13:7) Anywhere within their borders. That's a lot of ground to cover.

explanations.answer: Explain what the LORD did for them
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses says, “And on that day you are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.’” (Exodus 13:8) The feast comes with a story attached. The telling is part of the day.

explanations.answer: Teach them to bake the bread
explanations.explanation: A baking lesson would be right up my alley, but the text doesn't say it. Moses says they're to explain to their sons, “This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.” (Exodus 13:8) The job is telling, not baking. Still, I'd have paid good money to watch it.

No priests are mentioned in these verses. Moses tells the people to explain to their sons what the LORD did for them when they came out of Egypt (Exodus 13:8). The one doing the explaining is the person who lived it. That's a close, personal kind of teaching.
Not a one-time deal. Moses says, “Therefore you shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year.” (Exodus 13:10) Year after year, friend. That's a tradition, not a one-hit batch.
Right, it keeps coming back. Moses says, “Therefore you shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year.” (Exodus 13:10) Same time every year. It's a standing date on the calendar.
A lamb it is. Moses says, “You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb…” (Exodus 13:13) So the donkey is bought back, and a lamb is the price. It's a straight swap.

Grain isn't what the text names. Moses says, “You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb…” (Exodus 13:13) A lamb is the one on the list. Grain would be easier to carry, but that's not the deal.
Doves don't come up in these verses. Here the donkey is redeemed with a lamb: “You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb…” (Exodus 13:13) One lamb, no pair. That's all the verse asks.

That's not what the text says. Moses says, “…if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck.” (Exodus 13:13) That's a serious line. The donkey isn't kept for work, and that's why redeeming it with a lamb matters.
Right. Moses says, “…if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck.” (Exodus 13:13) It's a heavy line, and the text doesn't soften it. So the choice is redeem it with a lamb, or that.

explanations.answer: Because the LORD killed Egypt's firstborn
explanations.explanation: That's the answer, and it's a heavy one. Moses says, “…when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of man and beast.” (Exodus 13:15) Pharaoh was Egypt's king. That's why the Israelites give their firstborn animals to the LORD, and redeem their firstborn sons.

explanations.answer: Because Pharaoh demanded it as payment
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around. Pharaoh didn't demand anything here. He “stubbornly refused to let us go,” and then the LORD killed every firstborn in Egypt (Exodus 13:15). That's the reason given, and it's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: Because the firstborn led the march out
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say the firstborn led a march. The answer Moses gives goes back to when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let them go, and the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt (Exodus 13:15). It's a hard part of the story. That's why the answer to the son's question matters so much.

explanations.answer: They might face war and turn back
explanations.explanation: That's what God says. “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” (Exodus 13:17) The road through the Philistines' land was shorter, but it came with a risk. The Philistines were a people living on that road.

explanations.answer: The road ran too close to Pharaoh
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. God's reason is, “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” (Exodus 13:17) It's about what the people might do if they faced war. Pharaoh doesn't come into the reason.

explanations.answer: The Philistines had closed the road
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says the road was closed. It says the road was shorter, and that God didn't lead them that way because “If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt.” (Exodus 13:17) A shorter road isn't always the better one. I've learned that every time I've taken a shortcut to the oven.

explanations.answer: Through the wilderness toward the Red Sea
explanations.explanation: Yes. “So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea.” (Exodus 13:18) It's the long way around. God picked that road, and the people followed.

explanations.answer: East toward the land of Midian
explanations.explanation: Midian isn't named in these verses. The text says God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea (Exodus 13:18). That's the direction. East to Midian isn't in it.

explanations.answer: North through the hills of Moab
explanations.explanation: Moab doesn't show up here. The text says God led them “around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea.” (Exodus 13:18) It's a wilderness road, not a hill road. And a long one, too.
That's right. “…the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle.” (Exodus 13:18) They didn't leave empty-handed or unready. They walked out in battle order.
The text says they were. “…the Israelites left the land of Egypt arrayed for battle.” (Exodus 13:18) So they walked out ready, in battle order. Not a bunch of folks wandering out in their slippers.
That's it. “Moses took the bones of Joseph with him…” (Exodus 13:19) A special thing to pack for a long trip. Moses carries them out of Egypt.
The text names a different person. Moses took “the bones of Joseph,” not Jacob's (Exodus 13:19). Joseph is the one whose bones go along. Easy to mix up two names that go together.
Right name, wrong item. The verse says Moses took “the bones of Joseph with him,” not a coat (Exodus 13:19). Bones is what the text names. Quite a thing to pack, friend.

explanations.answer: Joseph made the sons of Israel swear
explanations.explanation: Yes. Moses took Joseph's bones “because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath…” (Exodus 13:19) It was a promise, and they kept it. A solemn oath is no small thing.

Pharaoh doesn't give that order. The text says Moses took the bones because “Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath…” (Exodus 13:19) The reason is a promise made to Joseph, not a command from Egypt's king.

explanations.answer: Aaron was told to in a dream
explanations.explanation: Aaron, Moses' brother (Exodus 4:14), isn't mentioned in this verse, and neither is any dream. The reason given is that “Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath…” (Exodus 13:19) It was a promise, plain and simple.
Yes. “And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day…” (Exodus 13:21) So by day, a cloud shows them the way. Nobody has to wonder which way to walk.

No star in this verse. By day, “the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide their way…” (Exodus 13:21) A cloud, not a star. I know stars well, since mine light up the sky over my bakery, but they're not the answer here.
No eagle here. The text says the LORD went before them “in a pillar of cloud to guide their way by day…” (Exodus 13:21) A cloud. Nothing with wings in this one.

Fire. The LORD went before them “in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night.” (Exodus 13:21) Cloud by day, fire by night. That's how they can keep going.

Lightning would be a lot to take in, but that's not the word. The text says “in a pillar of fire to give them light by night…” (Exodus 13:21) It's fire. Lightning would've been a short flash, not a steady light.

Water wouldn't give much light. The text says the LORD went before them “in a pillar of fire to give them light by night…” (Exodus 13:21) Fire is the word. Pillar of water would make for a soggy night walk.
It doesn't leave. “Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.” (Exodus 13:22) No breaks, no days off. It stays right in front of them.

Right, it stays put. “Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.” (Exodus 13:22) Day or night, it's there in front of them. No trip where they have to wonder where it went.
